Attent
at-tent'
a. (attentive; intent; heedful — an archaic form of attentive)
Latin attentus, from attendere, to stretch toward, from ad- and tendere. The picture is of a man leaning in — the ear stretched toward the speaker.

Biblical Definition

This archaic form of attentive occurs twice, and the two verses are a petition and its answer, separated by a chapter. At the dedication of the temple Solomon prays: “Now, my God, let, I beseech thee, thine eyes be open, and let thine ears be attent unto the prayer that is made in this place” (2Ch 6:40). Then the LORD appears to him by night and gives the answer back almost word for word: “Now mine eyes shall be open, and mine ears attent unto the prayer that is made in this place” (2Ch 7:15). The repetition is the point. God takes the king's own words and returns them as a promise, and the only change is from petition to declaration — let thine ears be becomes mine ears shall be. Solomon had already confessed that no house could contain Him — “the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house which I have built?” (2Ch 6:18) — so the promise is not that God is localized but that He has appointed a place where He undertakes to listen. And the condition attached is the famous one immediately before it: if my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines attent as attentive; intent; and marks it as obsolete in ordinary use, surviving chiefly in the Scripture phrase, let thine ears be attent.

ATTENT', a. [L. attentus.]

Attentive; intent.

Let thine ears be attent to the prayer that is made in this place. 2 Chron. 6.

The word is now obsolete in common discourse, being superseded by attentive.

From attendo, ad and tendo, to stretch toward; the ear stretched toward the speaker.

Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 6:40 — "Now, my God, let, I beseech thee, thine eyes be open, and let thine ears be attent unto the prayer that is made in this place."

2 Chronicles 7:15 — "Now mine eyes shall be open, and mine ears attent unto the prayer that is made in this place."

2 Chronicles 7:14 — "If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land."

2 Chronicles 6:18 — "But will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth? behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house which I have built!"

Modern Corruption

2 Chronicles 7:14 has been lifted out of this temple context and applied to modern nations as a covenant promise God never made to them.

expand to see more

The verse standing between these two occurrences — if my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves — is probably the most misapplied text in American religious life, printed on banners and quoted at rallies as a national promise. Its address is specific: it is spoken to Solomon about the temple just dedicated, to a people in covenant, whose land was given them by oath, and it concerns that house and that land. No modern nation stands in Israel's covenantal place. The dictionary does not on that account dismiss the verse; the God who said it has not changed, and humility, prayer, seeking His face and turning from wickedness are always the way sinners approach Him. But a promise made to a covenant people about a particular house is not a policy lever, and using it as one has taught a generation to expect national revival as a transaction.

The second corruption is more devotional and more common: reading God's attentiveness as unconditional and generic, as though He were obliged to hear anyone on any terms. 2 Chronicles 6:18 blocks that from the other side by confessing the transcendence — the heaven of heavens cannot contain Him, and it is pure condescension that He appoints any place at all. Under the new covenant the appointed place is not a building but a Person; access is through the one Mediator, and the ear stretched toward us was purchased. That is a better promise than Solomon had, and it is not a looser one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qashab (H7183), attentive, giving ear; oznayim qashuboth, ears attent; Latin attendere, to stretch toward.

expand to see more

Hebrew qashshuboth (H7183) — attentive, open to hear; 2 Chronicles 6:40 and 7:15, of the ears of God.

Hebrew qashab (H7181) — to prick up the ear, to incline and listen; the root, used of a man leaning toward a sound.

Hebrew kanaph … yikkane'u (H3665) — shall humble themselves, be brought low; 2 Chronicles 7:14.

Hebrew shemey hashamayim — the heaven of heavens; 2 Chronicles 6:18, which cannot contain Him.

Latin attentus, from ad- and tendere — stretched toward; Webster's root, now surviving only as attentive.

Usage

"“Let thine ears be attent” — Solomon's petition at the dedication."

"“Mine ears attent unto the prayer that is made in this place” — the same words, returned as promise."

"“The heaven of heavens cannot contain thee” — said by the man building Him a house."
